sprint-example.md at stage-1 does not contain the word 'velocity'; the lesson computes it from the last column.

Velocity (as this curriculum defines it, glossary 'velocity') = total story points of items that met the Definition of Done in one sprint; an unfinished item counts zero there and counts in the sprint that finishes it, so each point counts once.
The 2020 Scrum Guide (the official description of Scrum, where sprints come from) does not mention velocity or story points.
claims.source_hint: Scrum Guide 2020, full text (search for 'velocity', 'story point')

claims.text: Scrum Guide 2020, Sprint Planning (Topic Two): the more the Developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity, and their Definition of Done, the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts.
claims.source_hint: Scrum Guide 2020, Sprint Planning, Topic Two: What can be Done this Sprint?

claims.text: Story points are sized relative to a team's own earlier stories, so two teams' velocities are in different units and cannot be compared.

Counting an almost-done item as done describes a sprint that did not happen; an item that is almost done can still take days. A team pushed to raise its velocity tends to give bigger estimates while the work stays the same.

Velocity is one common practice teams add to record past performance, used at the next planning as a record of how much the team really finished; it is not required by Scrum. It compares a team with its own earlier sprints.
